sections.html:
In St. Croix County the treasurer's office does most of the work: it takes payments for 18 municipalities, accepts every second-half and late payment countywide, and keeps the tax rolls with assessed values. Visit the Government Center, 1101 Carmichael Road, Hudson, or phone 715-386-4645.

That office also prepares tax deed applications and handles credits. Valuation happens one level down. Your town, village or city clerk can tell you who your assessor is. If the name or parcel description on your bill looks wrong, the Real Property Listing office (715-386-4680) is the place to ask.

Each parcel gets a single statement a year, addressed to whoever owned it when bills were printed. A deed that changes hands afterward does not produce a second mailing. If you are buying in that gap, request a copy from the treasurer or the local clerk.

You can pay everything by January 31 or split the bill: half by January 31 and half by July 31. Wisconsin taxes run a year behind. A bill issued in December 2026 covers 2026 and becomes payable starting January 31, 2027. Expect the envelope in mid-December.

The rules sit in Wis. Stat. 74.11. A bill under $100 has to be settled in one payment by January 31. If the first half has not reached the office within five working days of January 31, the entire remaining balance goes delinquent on February 1. January 31, 2027 falls on a Sunday, so that five-day window closes at the end of business on Friday, February 5. Still, plan around January 31 itself, because payments count as on time when they are received by the due date.

Once a balance is delinquent the charge is 1.5% per month starting February 1, with any part of a month rounded up to a full one. The statute behind it, Wis. Stat. 74.47, fixes interest at 1% monthly and lets the county board tack on a penalty of up to 0.5% monthly. Payment plans are not offered here. Paying in part is still smart, and the law accepts partial payments of $20 or more against delinquent taxes.

sections.h2: Where to send the first installment
sections.html:
Where your check goes in January depends on where the parcel sits. Some municipalities route the first payment to the county treasurer, while others keep it locally. Here is a sample of the split.

MunicipalityWhere the first installment goes
City of Hudson, City of New Richmond, City of River FallsSt. Croix County Treasurer, 1101 Carmichael Rd, Hudson
Villages of Baldwin, Deer Park, Somerset and Star PrairieSt. Croix County Treasurer
Towns of Hudson, Richmond, Somerset, Star Prairie and StantonSt. Croix County Treasurer
City of Glenwood CityCity of Glenwood City Treasurer, 217 West Oak St
Village of North HudsonVillage of North Hudson Treasurer, 400 7th St N
Villages of Hammond, Roberts, Spring Valley, Wilson and WoodvilleThe village treasurer

Some towns, including Baldwin, Cady, Cylon and Emerald, also take their own January payment. No matter the municipality, the county treasurer receives July payments and anything overdue. A parcel in a place not shown above? Call 715-386-4645.

sections.h2: Ways to pay a St. Croix County bill
sections.html:
Pay by web portal, postal mail, the locked drop box or at the counter in the Government Center. The portal vendor adds $1.50 to an e-check and 2.99% to a debit or credit card.

  • Mail: write the parcel number on your check and address it to the collection point for your municipality. A stamped return envelope gets you a receipt.
  • Counter or drop box: bring the bill details with your payment. The box is at 1101 Carmichael Road.
  • Portal: look up the parcel by number, by address or by name, one search term at a time.

Mail a few days ahead of any deadline, because postal delays are your problem, not the county's. Need the bill sent somewhere else? The county has a change of address form.

sections.h2: How do you appeal a St. Croix County assessment?
sections.html:
Your first stop is the board of review run by your own town, village or city, not the county. Under Wis. Stat. 70.47 it convenes yearly during a 45-day stretch that begins the fourth Monday of April.

Before the meeting, the assessor must mail notice of a changed value: at least 15 days ahead normally, and 30 days ahead in a revaluation year. Missing the notice in your mailbox leaves the assessment standing. To object, work through this list:

  • Warn the board clerk, by voice or in writing, at least 48 hours before the opening meeting.
  • Hand the clerk a signed objection on the board's form during the first two hours of that meeting.
  • State, in writing, what you think the land is worth and what the improvements are worth, with the information behind your figures.
  • Testify under oath. Until you rebut it, the board assumes the assessor got the value right.

When land carries a house, you challenge one combined number rather than the lot or the building separately. Refusing the assessor's written request to look at the outside of the home costs you the right to testify.

For a home you live in, the biggest break is the state lottery and gaming credit. To get it you must be a Wisconsin resident who owns the dwelling and treats it as your primary residence on January 1. Nothing is automatic, so file for it. A credit that did not appear on your bill can still be claimed through the municipal treasurer by January 31, or late through the Department of Revenue by October 1.

Rental units, empty land and garages are out. At a sale the credit follows the parcel, which means it belongs in the tax proration between buyer and seller. The new owner, if living there, files a fresh application. Ask the county treasurer whether your parcel is receiving it.

Unpaid taxes can end in a tax deed taken by the county. Parcels it ends up owning are offered by sealed bid, with a 10% deposit, the balance due 30 days after the award, and a quit claim deed, as is.

You have choices long before that. Wis. Stat. 74.51 lets anyone clear delinquent taxes ahead of a tax certificate by paying what is due plus interest and any penalty. Under Wis. Stat. 74.53 the county may also take a former owner to court over taxes that went unpaid during that person's ownership, and co-owners share the liability.

Ask the treasurer for a payoff figure before listing. Give the number to your closing agent so it comes out of proceeds at closing and the buyer receives a clean parcel.

sections.h2: Selling a St. Croix County house
sections.html:
The county borders Minnesota, Hudson is its seat, and it belongs to the Minneapolis-St. Paul metro area. Population is 98,276 (2025 estimate), up 5.1% from April 2020. A typical owner-occupied home is valued at $377,700, and 78.3% of housing units are lived in by their owners.

A few errands help. Phone the treasurer for the current balance. Confirm who took the January payment, because it may have gone to a local treasurer while the July payment goes to the county. Keep your parcel number handy for every call. A cash buyer skips lender appraisal and financing delays, which helps when a payoff or deed problem is already eating the calendar.

faqs.q: When is the second installment due in St. Croix County?
faqs.a: July 31, paid to the St. Croix County Treasurer. If it is not received within five working days after that date, the entire unpaid balance goes delinquent August 1 under Wis. Stat. 74.11(8).

faqs.q: How much interest is charged on late property tax?
faqs.a: The charge is 1.5% a month counting from February 1, and a partial month is billed as a full one. State law sets the base at 1% monthly, and a county board may add as much as 0.5% as a penalty.

faqs.q: Can I set up a payment plan with the treasurer?
faqs.a: No, the office runs no payment plans. You are urged to pay whatever you can, and partial payments of $20 or more are accepted on delinquent taxes.

faqs.q: Who handles a property tax appeal?
faqs.a: Your municipal board of review. Tell its clerk at least 48 hours before the first meeting, then file a written objection in the first two hours. The board meets within a 45-day period that starts the fourth Monday of April.

faqs.q: Do I get a new tax bill if I buy a house after bills are printed?
faqs.a: No. Ownership changes recorded after printing produce no new statement, and the bill goes to the owner on record. As a buyer, ask the treasurer for a copy.
